title: Before every move: two questions
outcomes: Names what the opponent's last move threatens, including a checkmate threat
Finds one's own loose pieces, and knows when there is nothing to fix
Plays the first games with a simple routine and marks a moment of doubt

steps.text: Before every move, ask two questions. **1. What does my opponent's last move threaten?** (a capture, a check, a checkmate). **2. Is any of my pieces loose?** (attacked, and not defended). Only then choose your own move, and test it: after I move, what becomes capturable or exposed (the moved piece, a piece it stopped guarding, a line it opened)? Strong players do this all the time; many games are lost by skipping it.

steps.caption: White's queen and bishop aim at f7. If Black ignores this and develops a knight, Qxf7 is checkmate.

line.say: Black develops a knight and ignores the threat.

steps.title: The same attack, one defender more
steps.prompt: Black's knight went to h6, not f6. Predict first: does Qxf7 still win for White?

steps.text: The second question looks at your own side. After each opponent move, scan your pieces: is any of them attacked and not defended? If nothing is loose and nothing is threatened, you are free to follow your opening habits.

Now play your first games. Play simply: take the centre, bring your pieces out, castle, and ask the two questions before every move. Do not worry about winning. The goal is to notice. After a game, mark **one moment where you were unsure** and what you expected your opponent to do.

steps.prompt: After your first game: mark one move where you were unsure. What did you think your opponent would do there? You will compare your answer with what the game shows.
